new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls in Mouwase. The only prosodic information is that pitch is grammatically distinctive (negation marked by tone) in Ikobi, Mouwase and Barikewa per the 2009 SIL survey (example given from Ikobi only), and Usher's comparative site states, on the basis of Petterson's unpublished phonemic data, that tone is contrastive across the Omati River (Turama-Omatian) languages including Mouwase. Survey wordlists of Mouwase (Kibeni, Gibidai) are transcribed with pitch diacritics rather than stress marks.
new_statements.exceptions: none; Usher notes one Mouwase compound member as 'destressed' (vowel raising in *-dagu > -tuku 'elbow'), implying some stress asymmetry in compounds, without a rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Bullock's remark concerns grammatical (negation) tone on verb words, asserted jointly for three languages and exemplified from Ikobi (Moka village), not from Mouwase data; Usher's statement is family-level and second-hand. Neither addresses word stress or citation-form prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Mouwase = the Kibeni/Gibidai (and partly Omati-village Gihiteri) varieties of what Franklin 1973 and Ethnologue <17 called 'Omati' [mgx]; split by ISO CR 2011-081 into Mouwase [jmw]=mouw1234 and Barikewa [jbk]=bari1298. Johnston's 1921 'Karima' (Kibeni) list is Mouwase. Bullock 2015's tonal-negation remark is asserted for Ikobi, Mouwase and Barikewa jointly but exemplified only from Ikobi (ikob1240, Moka village). Usher's 'tone is contrastive' is stated for the whole Omati River (Turama-Omatian) group, resting on Petterson's unpublished Kaser/Mouwase materials.
